name: Tooth ablation

lead: Tooth ablation is the intentional removal of healthy teeth, typically upper incisors and canines, for reasons that include rites of passage, group identity, mourning and beauty ideals. In some societies a gap or altered smile was itself the mark of attractiveness or adulthood.

Archaeologists have found it in skeletons from Neolithic Taiwan and Jomon Japan, and ethnographers have recorded it across Africa, Asia and Oceania. The page records the practice as culture and history; it is not a recommended cosmetic procedure.

paras: Historically teeth were removed by elders or specialists with simple tools, usually during adolescence or as part of an initiation. Today dentists in some communities treat people who had teeth removed by providing partial dentures so the smile looks more conventional.
Reported consequences include pain, infection, retained roots, bone loss, bite changes and altered speech. Modern dental sources describe tooth removal for non-therapeutic reasons as irreversible.

chain: Culturally specified gap or altered smile
Appearance seen as beautiful or marking adult status in some societies
angle.text: In societies that practised it, the changed smile was the point: it signalled beauty, belonging or maturity. In modern dental terms it is a permanent alteration that clinicians restore with dentures.

lead: Tooth ablation, also called tooth evulsion, is the deliberate removal of healthy teeth. It has been recorded in many ancient and modern societies, for reasons including group identity, ornamentation and rites of passage such as coming of age, marriage and mourning.[1]

It targeted visible front teeth, so the result changed the appearance of the smile and lower face. Wikipedia notes that removing lower teeth would visibly change facial features and could affect pronunciation.[1] In some places beauty, fashion and peer pressure were named reasons.[1]

Archaeological evidence includes Neolithic skeletons from Taiwan, Jomon-period remains from Japan where ablation was particularly recorded among females, and later ethnographic accounts from Africa, Southeast Asia, the Pacific and Australia.[2][3][4]
infobox: Upper incisors and canines, sometimes lower
Rare; dentures provided where it persists

paras: Wikipedia says people in Formosa and mainland China practised tooth extraction before Austronesian peoples dispersed, and describes Nilotic customs among the Dinka, Nuer, Luo and Maasai, the Marquesas, Hawaii, the New Hebrides and Cape York.[1] The Dutch colonial government banned the Uma rite in Central Sulawesi in the early 1920s.[1] Jomon hunter-gatherers have been examined for how ablation relates to diet and time.[3] A 1993 British Dental Journal paper described a tooth ablation custom in the Maldives.[4]

Documented reasons include initiation into adulthood, beauty and fashion, group identification, mourning, magical beliefs and, in some accounts, aiding speech or feeding.[1] Practices were gender-specific in places: in the New Hebrides it was for girls, among the Maasai for boys.[1] Scholarly review of historical sex differences describes gender-related ablation of anterior teeth in skulls from history and prehistory.[2]

Wikipedia reports pain, infection risk, residual roots in the jaw and changes to eruption, occlusion and wear of remaining teeth. In South Africa dentists have fitted thousands of partial dentures to people wanting a more conventional appearance.[1]
No studies found. Relevant research is archaeological and anthropological.[2][3][4]
